# Inspection Authorization (IA) — Qualifications and Authority Regarding Major Alterations

Authority: Title 14, Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR, current issue), Part 65 Subpart D, read with Part 43 and Part 1. Framework: FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician (A&P) certification, 14 CFR Part 65.

---

## 0. Quick answer

1. The IA is **not a rating**. It is a separate authorization issued on top of a current A&P mechanic certificate (airframe + powerplant). Eligibility to obtain one is in **14 CFR 65.91**; term in **65.92**; renewal in **65.93**.
2. The qualification that specifically concerns **major alterations** is twofold:
   - **65.91(c)(5)** — the applicant must pass a written test on the ability to inspect per safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and after annual/progressive inspections under Part 43; and
   - **65.95(a)(1)** — the holder may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program) **after a major repair or major alteration**, *if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator*.
3. **The approved-technical-data condition is the whole ballgame.** An IA cannot approve a major alteration performed on unapproved data. The IA does not approve the *data*; the IA approves the *article for return to service*. Data approval is a separate act (FAA field approval, STC, DER/PMA/TSOA-approved data, or OEM data acceptable to the Administrator).
4. Major alterations must also be recorded on **FAA Form 337** (Part 43 Appendix B) and in the maintenance record (**43.9**), and approval for return to service must satisfy **43.5**.
5. Renewal (65.93) requires continued currency, and **major repairs or major alterations performed are themselves a renewal-credit currency route** (two per each 90 days the authorization was held).

---

Also note: the eCFR describes itself as **authoritative but unofficial**, updated daily and generally current within two business days. It is the correct working reference; the printed CFR remains the legal codification.

---

## 2. Qualifications to OBTAIN an inspection authorization — 14 CFR 65.91 (**R**)

| # | Requirement | Citation | Notes for major-alteration work |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold a **currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating**, each currently effective and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years** | 65.91(c)(1) | The 3-year clock runs on the ratings, not on employment. |
| 2 | Have been **actively engaged for at least the 2-year period before application** in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | 65.91(c)(2) | Must be maintenance of 14 CFR-certificated aircraft, not unrelated mechanical work. |
| 3 | Have a **fixed base of operations** at which the applicant may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week | 65.91(c)(3) | Need not be where the IA actually exercises the authorization. A change of base later triggers 65.95(c) (see §4). |
| 4 | Have **available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | 65.91(c)(4) | This is the facilities/data qualification that directly supports major-alteration approvals — you must be able to access the approved data. |
| 5 | **Pass a written test** on ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | 65.91(c)(5) | The only eligibility item expressly framed around major alterations. |
| 6 | Application made **on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator** | 65.91(a) | Currently FAA Form 8610-1 (Mechanic's Application for Inspection Authorization) — verify current form revision. |
| 7 | Retest bar: an applicant who fails the test may **not reapply for retesting until at least 90 days** after the date the application is denied or the test was failed, whichever is later | 65.91(d) | Hard 90-day bar. |

A person who meets all of the above is entitled to the authorization (65.91(b), **R**).

---

## 3. Term and renewal — 65.92 and 65.93 (**R**)

| Item | Requirement | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Term | IA is effective for **2 years** and **expires 31 March of each odd-numbered year** | 65.92 |
| Renewal window | Evidence must be presented **on or before 31 March of each odd-numbered year** | 65.93(a) |
| Continued eligibility | Applicant must still meet the requirements of **65.91(c)(1) through (4)** | 65.93(a) |
| Currency — option A | Perform **at least one annual inspection for each 90 days** the current authorization was held | 65.93(a)(1) |
| Currency — option B | Perform **at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the current authorization was held | 65.93(a)(2) |
| Currency — option C | Perform or supervise **at least two progressive inspections for each 90 days** the current authorization was held | 65.93(a)(3) |
| Currency — option D | Complete a **refresher or accredited course acceptable to the Administrator** within the 2 years preceding expiration | 65.93(a)(4) |

**Derived quantity check (approximation, shown so the arithmetic is auditable):** a full 2-year term ≈ 730 days; 730 ÷ 90 ≈ 8.1 90-day periods. Therefore a full-term renewal on option A is ≈ **8 annual inspections**; on option B ≈ **16 major repairs or major alterations**; on option C ≈ **16 progressive inspections**. These are derived from the regulation's per-90-day rate and are not themselves quoted numbers. Partial terms prorate.

**Direct relevance to the ask:** option B is the only renewal route denominated in major alterations, so an IA whose practice is predominantly major-alteration approval can satisfy currency through that work alone. Note the regulation counts **major repairs or major alterations performed**, which is not textually identical to "approved for return to service" — do not assume one-for-one credit without confirming with the responsible Flight Standards office.

---

## 4. Privileges and limitations governing major alterations — 14 CFR 65.95 (**V**)

Verbatim, current eCFR text (source: `http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95`, fetched 2026-11-15T04:13:13Z, sha256 04eedc455339):

> **§ 65.95 Inspection authorization: Privileges and limitations.**
>
> (a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
>
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
>
> (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.
>
> (b) When he exercises the privileges of an inspection authorization the holder shall keep it available for inspection by the aircraft owner, the mechanic submitting the aircraft, repair, or alteration for approval (if any), and shall present it upon the request of the Administrator or an authorized representative of the National Transportation Safety Board, or of any Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer.
>
> (c) If the holder of an inspection authorization changes his fixed base of operation, he may not exercise the privileges of the authorization until he has notified the responsible Flight Standards office or International Field Office for the area in which the new base is located, in writing, of the change.

Editorial note: the string `[New]` in (a)(1) is the eCFR's amendment-marker rendering for a recently revised cross-reference to Part 43. It is **not** part of the codified rule text; quote the section as "in accordance with part 43 of this chapter."

### 4.1 What 65.95(a)(1) decomposes into — four independent conditions

An IA's major-alteration approval is valid only if **all four** are satisfied. Any one failure voids the approval.

| # | Condition | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | The article is an **aircraft or related part or appliance** | Approving something outside the scope of "aircraft or related part or appliance." |
| C2 | The aircraft is **not** maintained under a **Part 121 continuous airworthiness program** | Signing off a Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft — outside IA authority; that work is approved under the operator's program (43.7 / Part 121). |
| C3 | The work was a **major repair or major alteration** performed **in accordance with Part 43** | Approving work performed outside Part 43 performance rules. |
| C4 | **The work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** | **The dominant disqualifier.** No Administrator-approved data = no IA approval authority, regardless of how good the workmanship is. |

### 4.2 What the IA is NOT authorized to do (derived from C4 and Part 43)

- **Approve the alteration data itself.** The IA does not issue field approvals, does not approve engineering, and does not "bless" a design. Data approval is a separate act by the FAA (field approval on Form 337 block 3), by an STC, by a DER under a delegation, or by use of OEM/TSOA/PMA data acceptable to the Administrator.
- **Approve for return to service a major alteration done on unapproved data** — for example, a modification whose only support is a mechanic's judgment, a manufacturer's non-approved service instruction used as alteration data, or an unincorporated drawing.
- **Approve a Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft** after major repair/alteration (express exclusion in 65.95(a)(1)).
- **Substitute for the performance authority.** 65.95(a)(1) grants inspection and return-to-service approval, not authority to perform the alteration; performance authority comes from 14 CFR 43.3 (mechanic certificate).

### 4.3 Independence question — flagged, not asserted

The text of 65.95 contains **no express prohibition** on an IA approving for return to service work the IA personally performed. Whether the responsible Flight Standards office or current FAA guidance imposes an independence restriction is a **policy** question, not a regulation-text question. Treat "an IA may not approve its own major alteration" as unverified until confirmed against current FAA order/AC guidance and local FSDO practice.

---

## 5. Gate 1 — Is it actually a "major alteration"? (Part 1 and Part 43 Appendix A) (**R**)

This determination is a prerequisite to everything in §4; if the work is minor, 65.95(a)(1) is not the operative authority.

**14 CFR 1.1 definition (R):** a *major alteration* is an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations. *Major repair* is defined in parallel terms.

**Part 43 Appendix A (R)** enumerates major alterations by category:
- (a) **Airframe** — e.g., wing spar replacement, changes to control surfaces/balance, structural changes, changes affecting weight and balance outside limits.
- (b) **Powerplant** — e.g., changes to powerplant installation affecting cooling, mounting, or exhaust; changes to fuel or ignition affecting operation.
- (c) **Propellers** — e.g., changes in diameter/pitch beyond specification, changes in propeller hub or blade design.
- (d) **Appliances** — e.g., changes to appliance design not in accordance with the appliance manufacturer's instructions.

The Appendix A list is illustrative-and-controlling; the Part 1.1 definition catches anything not enumerated. **Do not classify by intuition.** Classify by (i) checking the aircraft/engine/propeller specifications, then (ii) checking Appendix A, then (iii) applying the 1.1 appreciable-effect test.

---

## 6. Gate 2 — The approved-data path (**R**, with 65.95(a)(1) as the anchor)

| Data source | Approving party | IA may then approve RTS? |
|---|---|---|
| FAA field approval (Form 337, block 3 executed by FAA) | FAA | Yes |
| Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) | FAA | Yes, if the alteration conforms to the STC |
| Parts Manufacturer Approval (PMA) / TSOA article installed per its approved eligibility | FAA | Yes, per approved installation data |
| Designated Engineering Representative (DER) approved data under delegation | DER | Yes |
| OEM/TC-holder data acceptable to the Administrator | TC holder / Administrator | Yes, if acceptable to the Administrator for that alteration |
| No approved data (mechanic's judgment, unapproved service instruction, unincorporated drawing) | none | **No** — must obtain data approval first |

Key discipline: the IA's signature attests to **conformity with approved data and airworthiness**, not to the adequacy of the data.

---

## 7. Records and return-to-service mechanics (**R**)

| Requirement | Citation | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Persons authorized to approve RTS | 43.7 | A mechanic certificate holder may approve after maintenance/preventive maintenance/rebuilding/alteration; the **IA holder** is the person authorized to approve after a **major repair or major alteration**, subject to the approved-data condition. (Paragraph lettering to be confirmed on eCFR.) |
| Approval for RTS prerequisites | 43.5 | (a) required maintenance record entry made; (b) the repair/alteration form furnished/authorized by the Administrator executed as prescribed; (c) if operating limitations or AFM flight data change, those are revised per 91.9. |
| Maintenance record content | 43.9 | Description of work, date, name and certificate number of the person approving RTS; for major alterations, reference to the approved data used. |
| Major repair/alteration recording | Part 43 **Appendix B** | Requires **FAA Form 337** for major repairs and major alterations; one copy to the aircraft owner, one to the FAA. |
| Performance rules | 43.13 | Workmanship and methods acceptable to the Administrator; use of current data. |
| Inspection performance rules | 43.15 | Additional rules for annual/progressive inspections (supports 65.95(a)(2)). |

---

## 8. Operating procedure — IA approval of a major alteration (checklist)

| Step | Action | Authority | Record produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Confirm the IA is current and has not changed fixed base without written notice | 65.92, 65.95(c) | IA certificate; notice letter on file |
| 2 | Confirm the article is not a Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft | 65.95(a)(1) | — |
| 3 | Classify the work: minor vs. major alteration | 1.1; Part 43 App. A | Classification note in work package |
| 4 | If **minor**: no IA approval required; approve under mechanic authority as applicable | 43.7 | 43.9 logbook entry |
| 5 | If **major**: identify and verify the **Administrator-approved technical data** | 65.95(a)(1); 43.13 | Copy of STC/field approval/DER data in work package |
| 6 | If no approved data exists: **stop**; route for data approval (Form 337 field approval request to the FSDO/ASO, or STC/DER) | 65.95(a)(1) | Form 337 request package |
| 7 | Inspect the completed work for **conformity to the approved data** and for airworthiness | 65.95(a)(1); 43.13 | Inspection findings |
| 8 | Execute **FAA Form 337** | Part 43 App. B | Form 337, two copies |
| 9 | Make the maintenance record entry, referencing the approved data | 43.9; 43.5(a) | Logbook entry |
| 10 | If operating limitations or AFM flight data changed, ensure they are revised | 43.5(c); 91.9 | Revised AFM/limitations |
| 11 | Approve for return to service | 65.95(a)(1); 43.7 | Signature, certificate number, date |
| 12 | Record the event as renewal currency if using the major-alteration route | 65.93(a)(2) | Currency log |

## 10. Disqualifiers and common errors (practitioner summary)

1. **Approving a major alteration performed on unapproved data.** The single most common and most serious error. 65.95(a)(1) is conditional, not permissive.
2. **Treating the IA as a data-approval authority.** It is not. Field approval is an FAA act.
3. **Signing off a Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft.** Expressly excluded.
4. **Skipping Form 337.** Appendix B requires it for major repairs and major alterations.
5. **Omitting the approved-data reference from the 43.9 record entry.** Makes the approval unverifiable on its face.
6. **Failing to revise operating limitations/AFM data** when the alteration changes them (43.5(c), 91.9).
7. **Lapsed IA.** Exercising privileges after 31 March of an odd-numbered year without renewal is acting without authorization.
8. **Changed fixed base without written notice.** 65.95(c) suspends the privileges until notice is given — a purely administrative failure that voids the exercise of authority.
9. **Miscalculating the 3-year rating clock or the 2-year active-engagement window** at initial application, or the 90-day retest bar after a failure.
10. **Assuming a manufacturer's service bulletin or an unapproved drawing is "approved data."** It is not, absent FAA acceptance for that specific alteration.

---

- **"FAA-AMT"** is read as the FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician (A&P) certification framework under 14 CFR Part 65, in which the IA is an add-on authorization. - **Unverified items:** everything flagged **R**, plus the independence question in §4.3, plus the currency-credit question in §3 (whether "performed" and "approved for return to service" are treated identically for 65.93(a)(2) credit).

# Inspection Authorization (IA) qualifications as they bear on major alterations — FAA / 14 CFR part 65 (AMT context)

## 0. Answer in one line

The qualifications for an inspection authorization are set out in **14 CFR § 65.91(c)** (part 65, subpart D). For the major-alteration part of the question specifically, the operative element is **§ 65.91(c)(5)** — the applicant must pass a written test on inspecting to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** (and annual and progressive inspections) performed under part 43. Once issued, the authority to inspect and approve for return to service after a major alteration is **§ 65.95(a)(1)**, which is a *privilege*, not a qualification, and it does **not** include authority to approve the alteration *data*.

## 1. Source basis and confidence labels

| Label | Meaning | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **[Q]** quoted | Direct quoted passage in the research record | FAA IA Information Guide statements (part 121 exclusion; IA cannot approve data; § 65.95 is the functions section) |
| **[S]** summarized | Summarized from the research record's § 65.91(c) / § 65.95(a)(1) findings | The five eligibility elements; the return-to-service privilege |
| **[R]** recalled | Regulation content I am reproducing from knowledge of part 65/43 and that is **not** backed by a quoted passage in this record — confirm against eCFR before relying on it in a compliance decision | § 65.91(d), § 65.92, § 65.93(a), § 43.3/43.5/43.7 paragraph numbering, FAA Form 8610-1 |

Retrieval currency: the FAA IA Information Guide in the record was fetched 2026-11-15T04:15:19Z (sha256 ece24efe31ea). The eCFR pages were named as sources but could not be quoted directly in the record; treat eCFR text as the controlling text and re-pull it at the point of any actual determination.

Scope assumptions (stated, not hidden): US federal rules apply; "FAA-AMT" = the FAA aviation maintenance technician / part 65 mechanic-certificate context, not a document title; the question is answered as a research/citation answer, not as a determination on a specific alteration.

## 2. The qualification rule — § 65.91(c), element by element

An applicant who meets § 65.91(c) is *entitled* to an inspection authorization (§ 65.91(b)); the IA is an authorization added to a mechanic certificate, not a stand-alone certificate. All five elements must be satisfied simultaneously at the date of application.

| # | Requirement | Threshold / substance | Citation | Evidence to verify | Conf. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mechanic certificate with **both** Airframe **and** Powerplant ratings | Each rating currently effective **and** in effect for a total of **at least 3 years** | § 65.91(c)(1) | Airmen certificate + FAA airman registry record showing issue dates of each rating | [S] |
| 2 | **Actively engaged** in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter | For **at least the 2-year period** before the application date | § 65.91(c)(2) | Employer letters, work orders, logbook/337 records, training records — engagement, not mere employment | [S] |
| 3 | **Fixed base of operations** | A location at which the applicant can be reached in person or by telephone during a normal working week; need not be where the IA is exercised | § 65.91(c)(3) | Application form address + reachability attestation | [S] |
| 4 | **Equipment, facilities, and inspection data** available | Sufficient to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | § 65.91(c)(4) | Facilities/equipment inventory attestation; current maintenance manuals, ADs, TCDS, part 43, AC 43.13-1B/2B | [S] |
| 5 | **Written test** | Ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and **annual and progressive inspections** under part 43 | § 65.91(c)(5) | FAA test completion record | [S] |
| 6 | Retest wait after failure | May not reapply for testing until **90 days** after the failure date | § 65.91(d) | Test attempt record | [R] |

Application mechanics: application is made on the form and in the manner the Administrator prescribes (§ 65.91(a) [S]); in practice FAA Form 8610-1, *Mechanic's Application for Inspection Authorization* [R].

**Elements 1 and 2 are separate clocks and must not be merged.** The 3-year clock measures how long the airframe and powerplant ratings have been in effect; the 2-year clock measures active engagement in the 24 months immediately preceding application. Satisfying the 2-year engagement does not shorten the 3-year rating requirement, and holding the ratings for 10 years does not substitute for the 2-year engagement.

## 3. What "regarding major alterations" actually touches

A major alteration appears in four distinct places in the rule set. Confusing them is the single most common error in this subject.

### 3.1 It is a **test-content** qualification — § 65.91(c)(5)
The IA written test must cover inspection for return to service after major repairs and major alterations. This is a qualification element (you cannot get the IA without it). It does not, by itself, confer any authority.

### 3.2 It is a **privilege** after issuance — § 65.95(a)(1)
[Q] "With the exception of aircraft maintained in accordance with a Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program under part 121, an IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance after a major repair or major alteration." [S] The privilege is conditioned on the work having been done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**.

Two hard limits fall out of that sentence and must be stated in any answer on this topic:
- **Part 121 CAMP exclusion.** Aircraft maintained under a part 121 continuous airworthiness maintenance program are outside the IA's major-repair/major-alteration return-to-service authority.
- **Approved-data precondition.** No approved technical data ⇒ no IA return-to-service approval of the major alteration.

### 3.3 It is **not** a data-approval authority
[Q] "The holder of an IA *cannot* approve the *data* for major repairs or major alterations." The IA inspects conformity to previously approved data; the IA does not create or approve the alteration data (that is a part 21 / design-approval function — field approval, STC, or other approved data).

### 3.4 It drives **records**
Return to service after a major repair or major alteration requires the maintenance record entry and the repair/alteration form furnished by the Administrator (FAA Form 337) to be executed, and any resulting operating-limitation or flight-manual change to be reflected — § 43.5 [R]; record content § 43.9 [R]; major-alteration record-keeping § 43.9(d) [R]. "Major alteration" itself is defined in **14 CFR part 1** [S/R] and enumerated by product type (airframe / engine / propeller) in **part 43, Appendix A** [R]. Part 43 Appendix A and the part 1 definition determine *whether* the work is a major alteration; part 65 determines *who* may inspect it and sign it off.

### 3.5 Summary matrix — who may do what

| Action | Certificated A&P mechanic (no IA) | IA holder |
|---|---|---|
| Perform a major alteration | Yes, within ratings, per § 43.3 [R] | Yes |
| Approve for return to service after a major alteration | **No** | **Yes**, except part 121 CAMP aircraft, and only if done to Administrator-approved technical data (§ 65.95(a)(1)) |
| Approve the alteration *data* | No | **No** (per FAA IA Information Guide) |
| Perform/approve an annual inspection; perform or supervise a progressive inspection | No | Yes (§ 65.95(a)(2)) [R] |

## 4. Duration and renewal (secondary, but part of the qualification picture)

| Item | Requirement | Citation | Conf. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expiration | March 31 of each **odd-numbered year** (2-year cycle), or on surrender/suspension/revocation | § 65.92 [R] | [R] |
| Renewal window | Evidence presented on or before **March 31** of the renewal year | § 65.93(a) [R] | [R] |
| Renewal activity (any **one** of — OR gate, not cumulative), within the **24 months** before application | (1) at least **1** annual inspection; or (2) at least **2** major repairs **or** major alterations; or (3) performed or supervised and approved at least **1** progressive inspection; or (4) a refresher course of not less than **8 hours** of instruction acceptable to the Administrator; or (5) an oral test by an FAA inspector | § 65.93(a)(1)–(5) [R] | [R] |

Note the asymmetry that a test engineer must not gloss over: the **initial** qualification requires the written test on major alterations (§ 65.91(c)(5)), while **renewal** can be satisfied by *performing* two major repairs or major alterations (§ 65.93(a)(2)) with no test at all. A renewal checklist that demands a test is wrong; a renewal checklist that accepts one major alteration plus one annual inspection as satisfying (a)(2) is also wrong — (a)(1) and (a)(2) are separate alternative routes, and the pair satisfies (a)(1) only.

## 5. Deterministic eligibility calculator (desk-checkable)

Use these formulas so two reviewers reach the same pass/fail. All dates inclusive of the application date, ISO format.

```
R1_PASS  = (years_between(AF_issue, app_date) >= 3) AND (years_between(PP_issue, app_date) >= 3)
           where years_between(a,b) = (b - a) in years, fractional, no rounding up
           AF_current = AF rating shown as effective on airman record at app_date
           PP_current = PP rating shown as effective on airman record at app_date

R2_PASS  = documented_engagement_days(window_start, app_date) >= 730  OR  >= 731 in a leap-spanning window
           window_start = app_date minus 24 months
           Count only days of ACTIVE ENGAGEMENT in maintaining aircraft certificated and
           maintained under the chapter. Gaps subtract. Employment without engagement does not count.

R3_PASS  = fixed_base_address_present AND reachable_by_phone_during_normal_working_week

R4_PASS  = equipment_inventory_attested AND inspection_data_current
           (data set must include, at minimum: manufacturer maintenance manuals for the products
            to be inspected, current ADs, TCDS, 14 CFR parts 1/43/65/91, AC 43.13-1B and -2B)

R5_PASS  = written_test_passed AND test_record_date >= (prior_failure_date + 90 days) if any prior failure

ISSUE    = R1_PASS AND R2_PASS AND R3_PASS AND R4_PASS AND R5_PASS
```

### Worked examples (all arithmetic shown)

**Example A — pass on ratings.** Application 2025-03-14. Airframe rating issued 2019-08-02 → 5 y 224 d ≈ **5.61 y** ≥ 3. Powerplant rating issued 2021-11-30 → 3 y 104 d ≈ **3.29 y** ≥ 3. → **R1 PASS.** (Note the certificate may be older than the second rating; the test is per-rating, so the newly added rating governs.)

**Example B — fail on ratings.** Application 2025-03-14. Powerplant rating issued 2023-01-20 → 2 y 53 d ≈ **2.15 y** < 3. → **R1 FAIL.** Earliest eligible application date = 2023-01-20 + 3 y = **2026-01-20**. Do not round 2.15 up to 3.

**Example C — one-day failure on engagement.** Application 2025-03-14 → 24-month window opens **2023-03-14**.
- Engagement 2023-03-14 → 2025-03-14 = **731 days** = full window → **R2 PASS**.
- Engagement 2023-03-15 → 2025-03-14 = **730 days** = **short by 1 day** → **R2 FAIL** (leap day 2024-02-29 is inside the window; the day count above already includes it).

**Example D — renewal OR gate.** In the 24 months before renewal application the holder performed 1 major alteration and 1 major repair, and no annual inspection. → § 65.93(a)(2) satisfied (**two** major repairs or major alterations) → renewal activity **PASS**. If instead the holder had 1 major alteration and 1 annual inspection, (a)(2) is **not** satisfied by the alteration alone, but (a)(1) is satisfied by the annual → still PASS, by a different route. If the holder had 1 major alteration only and nothing else → (a)(1)–(a)(3) all fail → must use the 8-hour refresher (a)(4) or the FAA oral test (a)(5).

## 6. Desk/bench test protocol IA-ELIG-01 (procedure a competent engineer or DME-equivalent reviewer can run)

**Purpose:** determine, reproducibly, whether an applicant is qualified for an IA and, separately, whether a proposed major-alteration approval is within the IA privilege.

**Part A — Qualification audit**
1. Pull the airman record. Record the issue date of the airframe rating and of the powerplant rating separately. Verify both are currently effective. Compute R1 per § 5. Record pass/fail and, on fail, the earliest eligible date.
2. Build a dated engagement timeline for the 24 months preceding the application date. Mark each interval as engagement / non-engagement. Sum engagement days. Compare to the window length. Record pass/fail and the exact shortfall in days.
3. Verify fixed base of operations and normal-working-week reachability. Pass/fail.
4. Verify the equipment/facilities/inspection-data inventory against the minimum data set in § 5 R4. Pass/fail per line item.
5. Verify the written test record and, if any prior failure exists, that the retest occurred ≥ 90 days later. Pass/fail.
6. Issue a single verdict: ISSUE only if all five are PASS. Any FAIL blocks issuance and must name the earliest date the element can be cured.

**Part B — Major-alteration privilege audit (per job)**
1. Classify the work: major alteration vs minor alteration, using the part 1 definition and part 43 Appendix A for the specific product type (airframe / engine / propeller). If minor, the IA privilege is not the operative rule.
2. Confirm approved technical data exists and covers the alteration. If not → **STOP**, the IA cannot approve return to service.
3. Confirm the aircraft is **not** maintained under a part 121 continuous airworthiness maintenance program. If it is → **STOP**, out of scope of § 65.95(a)(1).
4. Confirm the IA physically inspected the work and that the conformity inspection was performed. Record the inspection method and the data referenced.
5. Confirm the record set: maintenance record entry (§ 43.9), repair/alteration form (FAA Form 337) executed, and any operating-limitation / flight-manual change captured. If any is missing → **FAIL**, do not return to service.
6. Explicitly record that the IA did **not** approve the alteration data. Any file in which the IA signature appears as data approval is a finding.

1. Answering with § 65.95 when the question asks for *qualifications* — § 65.95 is privileges.
2. Saying the IA "approves major alterations" without the two conditions (approved data; not part 121 CAMP).

# Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — 14 CFR Qualification Analysis

**Ask answered:** What are the qualifications for inspection authorization regarding major alterations (FAA-AMT context), using eCFR as the source.

---

## 0. Interpretation applied (state it, so the answer can be checked)

- **“inspection auth” = Inspection Authorization (IA)** under 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D (§§ 65.91–65.95). It is *not* generic return-to-service authority under Part 43, *not* a Part 121/135 Required Inspection Item (RII) designation, and *not* a designee/DER delegation.
- **“qualifications … regarding major alterations” is answered at two levels**, because the regulation splits them across two sections and both must be satisfied:
  - **Level 1 — eligibility to hold the IA** (§ 65.91).
  - **Level 2 — the conditions attached to using the IA on a major alteration** (§ 65.95(a)(1), plus the Part 43 companions in § 4 below).
- **“FAA-AMT”** is read as the FAA aviation maintenance technician domain (A&P mechanics and IA applicants/exercisers); the AMT-specific framing is in § 8.
- **Assumed:** U.S. 14 CFR, current eCFR text; Part 91 operator unless stated otherwise; “major alteration” as defined in § 1.1 and listed in Appendix A to Part 43. If the aircraft is maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, the IA privilege in § 65.95(a)(1) does **not** apply — see § 5.

---

## 1. Short answer — the qualifications, in order

| # | Qualification | Rule | Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, **each effective for at least 3 years** | § 65.91(c)(1) | Eligibility |
| 2 | Have been **actively engaged in the maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration of aircraft during the preceding 2 years** | § 65.91(c)(1) | Eligibility |
| 3 | Have a **fixed base of operations** at which the applicant may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week (need not be where the IA is exercised) | § 65.91(c)(2) | Eligibility |
| 4 | Have available the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | § 65.91(c)(3) | Eligibility |
| 5 | **Pass a written test** on ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | § 65.91(c)(4) | Eligibility |
| 6 | At the moment of use on a specific major alteration: the work must have been done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**, in accordance with Part 43, and the aircraft must **not** be maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program | § 65.95(a)(1) | Exercise |

Two supporting qualifications are frequently tested and frequently missed:

| # | Qualification | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | **Recent experience:** no exercise of mechanic privileges unless, within the preceding 24 months, the Administrator has found the holder able to do the work, or the holder has at least 6 months in one of the listed capacities (served as a mechanic under the certificate and rating; technically supervised other mechanics; supervised maintenance/alteration in an executive capacity; engaged in inspection of aircraft) | § 65.83 |
| 8 | **Unbroken currency of the authorization itself:** the IA expires on **March 31 of each odd-numbered year** and must be renewed | §§ 65.92, 65.93 |

---

## 2. Level 1 — eligibility to hold an IA (§ 65.91)

Structure of the section, as written:

- **§ 65.91(a)** — application is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator.
- **§ 65.91(b)** — an applicant who meets the requirements of the section **is entitled** to an inspection authorization. (Entitlement language: meeting the criteria is the whole test; there is no discretionary “fit and proper” gate in this section.)
- **§ 65.91(c)** — the four eligibility items:

**(c)(1) Certificate and engagement.**
- Both ratings required. An **airframe-only or powerplant-only** mechanic is **not eligible**. This is the single most common AMT exam error on this section.
- Each rating must have been **effective for at least 3 years** (measured from the rating date on the certificate, not from the date the certificate was issued).
- Plus: **actively engaged** in the maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration of aircraft **during the preceding 2 years**.
- Note that (c)(1) speaks to *maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration* — not to *inspection*. Inspection experience is not the statutory prerequisite for initial eligibility; it becomes relevant at renewal (§ 6).

**(c)(2) Fixed base of operations.**
- Must be locatable **in person or by telephone during a normal working week**.
- Expressly **need not** be the place where the IA will be exercised. This is a reachability requirement, not a shop-location requirement.

**(c)(3) Equipment, facilities, and inspection data.**
- Must be **available** to the holder: equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
- This is the eligibility counterpart of the “approved technical data” condition in § 65.95(a)(1); the IA cannot lawfully sign a major alteration he has no data to inspect against.

**(c)(4) Written test — the direct major-alteration hook.**
- The test is on the applicant’s **ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43.
- This is why “IA” and “major alterations” are coupled in the regulation itself: the examination scope is defined by the major repair/major alteration return-to-service decision, not by general maintenance skill.

**(d) Retest wait.** An applicant who fails the test may not apply for retesting until a specified waiting period has elapsed after the failure date. *(Figure flagged for verbatim confirmation in § 11 — do not quote the day count from this document without checking the current eCFR text.)*

---

## 3. Level 2 — the privilege and the conditions on major alterations (§ 65.95)

**Verbatim, § 65.95(a) (eCFR, Part 65 Subpart D):**

> “(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
> (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.”

**Decompose (a)(1) into its four conditions.** All four must hold before the IA signs:

1. **Subject matter** — an aircraft or a related part or appliance.
2. **Part 121 carve-out** — **not** an aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121. The IA privilege is unavailable for those aircraft; the certificate holder’s own release system governs (§ 5).
3. **Work classification and rules** — the work is a **major repair or major alteration**, accomplished **in accordance with Part 43** (i.e., §§ 43.3, 43.5, 43.9, 43.13, and Appendix A/B).
4. **Data condition** — the work was done **in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**. This is the condition most often failed in practice: an alteration accomplished on unapproved or merely “acceptable” data cannot be approved for return to service by an IA under this paragraph, no matter how good the workmanship.

**What § 65.95 does *not* give the IA:**
- No authority to **approve data**. The IA inspects and approves for return to service; he does not create approved technical data. Data approval runs through the TC/STC, PMA, field-approval, or DER channels.
- No authority to approve a Part 121 aircraft for return to service under (a)(1).
- No authority to substitute for a certificate holder’s airworthiness release under Part 121/135.

**§ 65.95(b) and (c)** impose conditions on the *manner* of exercise (presence at the inspection, availability of data and equipment, and the limits on supervision). Those paragraphs are flagged for verbatim confirmation in § 11 rather than paraphrased here, because the exact wording is what an enforcement action would turn on.

---

## 4. Part 43 obligations that travel with the IA signature

The IA privilege is the *authority* to sign; Part 43 is the *substance* of what is being signed. A complete answer to “qualifications regarding major alterations” includes these, because failing any of them makes the IA’s approval invalid even though the IA itself was properly held.

**4.1 Determine major vs. minor first.**
- **§ 1.1 definition:** a **major alteration** is an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications — (1) that might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) that is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
- **Appendix A to Part 43** lists major alterations by product category (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance) and lists major repairs. If the change appears on the list, it is major. If it does not appear, apply the § 1.1 test.
- The IA qualification attaches only once the work is classified as a major repair or major alteration. A minor alteration is approved under the ordinary mechanic return-to-service rules.

**4.2 Approved technical data.** Required by § 65.95(a)(1). Accepted sources include type certificate data, supplemental type certificates, parts manufacturer approvals installed per their approval, data approved under a field approval, and DER-approved data. An IA may not “bless” an alteration by inspecting it after the fact if the data were never approved.

**4.3 Form 337 (Appendix B to Part 43).** A major repair or major alteration must be recorded on the repair and alteration form furnished by the Administrator (FAA Form 337), executed as prescribed. The IA’s approval-for-return-to-service signature on the form is the act § 65.95(a)(1) authorizes.

**4.4 Maintenance record entry (§ 43.9).** The record must contain a description of the work, the date of completion, the name of the person performing the work, and, if the work was done under an approval, a reference to that approval (e.g., the STC or field approval).

**4.5 Operating limitations / AFM (§ 91.9 by way of Part 43).** If the alteration changes operating limitations or flight data in the approved AFM, those limitations and data must be revised and set forth as prescribed.

**4.6 Return-to-service preconditions (Part 43 Subpart C).** No person may approve for return to service an aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, or appliance that has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration unless:

> “(a) The maintenance record entry required by § 43.9 or § 43.11, as appropriate, has been made;
> (b) The repair or alteration form authorized by or furnished by the Administrator has been executed in a manner prescribed by the Administrator; and
> (c) If a repair or an alteration results in any change in the aircraft operating limitations or flight data contained in the approved aircraft flight manual, those operating limitations or flight data are appropriately revised and set forth as prescribed in § 91.9 of this chapter.”

*(This precondition text sits in Part 43 Subpart C; the internal lettering differs between codification years — confirm the subparagraph letters at the eCFR page cited in § 10 before quoting letters in a training product.)*

**4.7 Perform vs. approve.** These are separate acts. A certificated mechanic **may perform** a major alteration. A mechanic **without** an IA **may not approve it for return to service** — that is the specific gap the IA fills for individuals. The mechanic’s return-to-service authority under Part 43 is limited to work other than a major repair or major alteration.

---

## 5. When the IA is *not* the required approver

An IA is one of several routes to approving a major alteration. § 43.7 lists the persons authorized to approve for return to service; among them are the certificated mechanic (limited, not for major repairs/alterations), the **holder of an inspection authorization**, the **holder of a repair station certificate** (Part 145), the **holder of an air carrier or operating certificate** (Parts 121/135), and the **holder of a production certificate** for the products it manufactured. So the correct compliance statement is: *for an individual mechanic in general aviation, the IA is the route; for a certificate holder, the certificate holder’s own system is the route.*

**Part 121.** § 65.95(a)(1) expressly excludes aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. Those aircraft are released under the carrier’s airworthiness release system: § 121.709 (airworthiness release or aircraft log entry) requires a release or log entry before the aircraft may be operated after maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alterations.

**Part 135.** § 135.443 imposes the parallel airworthiness release / aircraft maintenance log entry requirement.

**RII overlay (both).** Part 121 carriers must have a Required Inspection Item program under § 121.369 — the manual must include RII procedures and a list of RII items, and only persons authorized by the certificate holder may perform and approve those inspections. Part 135 operators have corresponding manual requirements. **RII authority is a certificate-holder designation, not an IA privilege**; holding an IA does not confer RII authority, and RII authority does not confer IA privileges.

---

## 6. Currency, duration, and renewal (including the major-alteration renewal credit)

**6.1 Recent experience (§ 65.83).** A certificated mechanic may not exercise the privileges of the certificate and rating unless, within the preceding 24 months, the Administrator has found the holder able to do the work, or the holder has at least 6 months in one of the listed capacities (served as a mechanic under the certificate and rating; technically supervised other mechanics; supervised maintenance or alteration in an executive capacity; engaged in some capacity in the inspection of aircraft).

**6.2 Duration (§ 65.92).** The inspection authorization expires on **March 31 of each odd-numbered year** — a fixed two-year cycle tied to the calendar, not to the holder’s anniversary date.

**6.3 Renewal (§ 65.93).** To renew for a two-year period, the holder must present evidence during March of the odd-numbered year of one of the following:

| Option | Requirement |
|---|---|
| (a)(1) | At least **one annual inspection for each 90 days** the holder was actively engaged in performing inspections under Part 65 during the preceding 24 months |
| (a)(2) | At least **two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the holder was actively engaged in performing inspections under Part 65 during the preceding 24 months |
| (a)(3) | At least **one progressive inspection performed or supervised and approved** for each 90 days of such active engagement |
| (a)(4) | Attendance at and successful completion of a **refresher course acceptable to the Administrator of not less than 8 hours** during the preceding 24 months |

**This is the second direct link between IA and major alterations:** major repairs and major alterations are a *countable renewal activity* in their own right under (a)(2), at a rate of two per 90 days of active engagement. An IA whose work is predominantly major-alteration approval can renew on that basis without doing annual inspections.

*(Subparagraph lettering in § 65.93 flagged for confirmation in § 11; the four options and their rates are the substance.)*

---

## 7. Applying it — compliance checklist for one specific major alteration

Run this in order. Any “no” is a stop.

1. **Classify.** Is the change a major alteration under § 1.1 / Appendix A to Part 43? Document the basis.
2. **Data.** Is there technical data **approved by the Administrator** covering the alteration as installed? Identify the approval (TC, STC, field approval, DER-approved data). If not — stop; the IA cannot approve under § 65.95(a)(1).
3. **Aircraft status.** Is the aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program? If yes — stop; the IA privilege does not reach it.
4. **Holder’s currency.** Is the IA currently effective (not expired on the last March 31 of an odd-numbered year)? Does the holder meet § 65.83 recent experience?
5. **Holder’s capability for this job.** Does the holder have the equipment, facilities, and inspection data for this product (§ 65.91(c)(3))? Is he physically present at the location where the inspection is performed, as § 65.95 requires?
6. **Performance.** Was the work performed by a person authorized under Part 43, using the methods, techniques, and practices of § 43.13?
7. **Inspection.** Inspect against the approved data — conformity to the data is the test, not “looks airworthy.”
8. **Records.** Make the § 43.9 entry; execute FAA Form 337 per Appendix B to Part 43; revise AFM limitations/flight data if affected.
9. **Return to service.** Sign the approval for return to service only after steps 1–8 are complete.
10. **Distribution.** Forward the Form 337 per the form’s instructions and Appendix B (FAA copy and owner copy). *(The forwarding time limit is flagged in § 11.)*

---

## 8. AMT framing (the “FAA-AMT” tag)

- **For the A&P studying for the IA:** the qualification set is the § 1 table above. The exam-relevant points are that (i) **both** ratings are required, (ii) each rating must be **3 years** old, (iii) the **2-year active engagement** window is separate from the 3-year rating age, and (iv) the **written test scope is defined by major repairs and major alterations**, not by general maintenance.
- **For the working AMT:** the practical rule is that a mechanic can *do* a major alteration but only an IA (or a certificate holder under § 43.7) can *approve* it for return to service — and only if the data were approved and the aircraft is not a Part 121 aircraft.
- **For the IA renewing:** major repairs and major alterations count at **two per 90 days** of active engagement (§ 65.93(a)(2)), as an alternative to the annual-inspection route.
- **Study sources beyond the rule text:** AC 43-9C (Maintenance Records), AC 43.9-1G (Instructions for Completion of FAA Form 337), AC 43-210A (Standardized Procedures for Requesting Approval of Data for Major Repairs and Major Alterations), AC 120-16 (Air Carrier Maintenance Programs) for the Part 121/135 side, and the FAA AMT handbooks (General, Airframe, Powerplant) for the underlying systems knowledge.

---

## 9. Frequent errors this analysis is written to prevent

| Error | Correction |
|---|---|
| Treating “inspection authorization” as any authority to inspect | It is a specific Part 65 Subpart D authorization with defined eligibility and defined privileges |
| Believing an A&P alone can approve a major alteration | A mechanic may perform it; approval for return to service after a major repair/alteration requires an IA (or a § 43.7 certificate holder) |
| Believing an IA can approve anything, anywhere | § 65.95(a)(1) excludes Part 121 aircraft; RII authority is separate and comes from the certificate holder |
| Believing the IA can approve the *data* | The IA approves the *work* for return to service; the data must already be approved by the Administrator |
| Quoting “3 years” as the experience requirement without the 2-year engagement clause | Both are in § 65.91(c)(1) and both apply |
| Assuming an airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic qualifies | Both ratings, each 3 years effective, are required |
| Forgetting Form 337 | It is a separate, mandatory recording step under Appendix B to Part 43, distinct from the § 43.9 log entry |

answer:
REGULATORY ENGINEER RESPONSE — IA QUALIFICATIONS AS THEY RELATE TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS

0. SCOPE AND INTERPRETATION
The question admits two readings, and both are answered below because the regulation treats them separately:
  Reading A — What must a person qualify for/hold in order to obtain an Inspection Authorization (IA), insofar as major alterations are concerned?  -> 14 CFR 65.91, 65.92, 65.93 (Part 65, Subpart D).
  Reading B — What is the IA's authority/limitation with respect to major alterations once held?  -> 14 CFR 65.95 and Part 43.
Primary source: eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 65, Subpart D (ecfr.gov). Definition source: 14 CFR 1.1 and Appendix A to Part 43. Non-regulatory guidance is segregated in Section 9.

1. THRESHOLD DEFINITION — WHAT COUNTS AS A 'MAJOR ALTERATION'
All IA qualification/authority questions key off this classification, so it is stated first.
  14 CFR 1.1: 'Major alteration' means an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications — (1) that might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) that is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations. 'Minor alteration' means an alteration other than a major alteration.
  Appendix A to Part 43 (Major Alterations, Major Repairs, and Preventive Maintenance) enumerates alterations in airframe, powerplant, propeller, and appliance categories that are major.
  Practical consequence: the IA qualification/authority described below attaches to the major side of that line. Minor alterations do not require an IA.

2. READING A — QUALIFICATIONS TO OBTAIN AN INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (14 CFR 65.91)
Section 65.91(c) sets the complete eligibility list. An applicant must satisfy all five:
  (c)(1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective.
  (c)(2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 3-year period before the date of application, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with 14 CFR Chapter I.
  (c)(3) Have a fixed base of operations at which the applicant may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week (it need not be the place where the IA will be exercised).
  (c)(4) Have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
  (c)(5) Pass a written test on the applicant's ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after MAJOR REPAIRS and MAJOR ALTERATIONS and for annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43.
This is the direct answer to the question as posed: the major-alteration-specific qualification element is 65.91(c)(5) — demonstrated, tested competence in inspecting and returning to service aircraft after major repairs and major alterations — supported by (c)(1) (both ratings), (c)(2) (3 years of practical experience), (c)(4) (access to the inspection data needed to judge conformity to approved data), and the administrative prerequisites in (c)(3).

3. MAINTAINING THE QUALIFICATION (CURRENCY) — 14 CFR 65.92 AND 65.93
  65.92: each inspection authorization expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year (biennial rating cycle).
  65.93(a) [paraphrase]: the holder may exercise IA privileges only while holding a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe rating and a currently effective powerplant rating.
  65.93(b) renewal — the applicant must, in addition to meeting the underlying requirements, show recent major-alteration/major-repair activity. Verified regulatory text includes: '(2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority.' Section 65.93(b) also provides alternative renewal paths in its remaining subparagraphs; read the full paragraph at the cited eCFR section rather than relying on this summary for those alternatives.
  Interpretation note for AMT context: the renewal standard is the regulation's own mechanism for keeping the IA's major-alteration competence current — the activity it counts is major repair/major alteration work, not routine servicing.

4. READING B — THE IA'S AUTHORITY OVER MAJOR ALTERATIONS (14 CFR 65.95)
  65.95(a)(1) (verbatim): the holder of an inspection authorization may 'Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.'
  Three conditions are embedded in that single sentence and must all hold before an IA signs:
    (i) The work is a major repair or major alteration within Part 43;
    (ii) The work was accomplished using technical data approved by the Administrator (not merely acceptable data, and not data the IA itself 'approves');
    (iii) The aircraft is not maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program — that exclusion is written into the privilege.
  65.95(a)(2) [paraphrase]: the IA may also perform an annual inspection, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection, per 43.11, 43.12 and 91.409. This is a separate privilege from the major-alteration approval privilege and is not a qualification for it.
  Section 65.95's remaining paragraphs impose additional limitations on the exercise of these privileges; they should be read in full at the eCFR section before use in an enforcement-sensitive context.

5. WHAT THE IA DOES *NOT* CONFER (common AMT exam and ramp-error point)
  - An IA is an inspection/approval authority, not a super-mechanic certificate. Authority to PERFORM an alteration comes from 14 CFR 43.3 (persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations — e.g., a certificated mechanic with the appropriate rating) and, for the IA holder, from the underlying mechanic certificate.
  - An IA does not approve technical data. Approved data comes from the Administrator (e.g., STC, TC changes, field approvals, or data FAA has approved); the IA's job is to verify the alteration conforms to that approved data.
  - Approval for return to service after maintenance/alteration is governed by 14 CFR 43.7 (persons authorized to approve for return to service); the IA's major-alteration route through that section is 65.95(a)(1).

6. PART 43 DUTIES AN IA MUST APPLY WHEN SIGNING A MAJOR ALTERATION
  43.5 [paraphrase] — approval for return to service only after the required maintenance/alteration has been performed.
  43.9 — maintenance record content, including the description of work, date, and the signature/certificate number of the person approving for return to service.
  43.13(a)/(b) — use current manufacturer's methods/techniques/practices (or other methods acceptable to the Administrator) and perform the work so the condition is at least equal to its original or properly altered condition.
  Appendix B to Part 43 — Recording of Major Repairs and Major Alterations: the FAA Form 337 recording requirement that accompanies a major alteration.
  91.417(a)(2) [paraphrase] — the operator's maintenance records must include copies of the forms prescribed by 43.9(d) for each major alteration to the airframe and currently installed components. (Owner/operator recordkeeping, not an IA qualification, but it is the record the IA's approval feeds.)
  65.83 [paraphrase] — SEPARATE mechanic-certificate recent-experience rule: within the preceding 24 months the mechanic must have, for at least 6 months, served as a mechanic under the certificate and rating, technically supervised other mechanics, supervised maintenance/alteration in an executive capacity, or a combination. This is a mechanic-certificate requirement and is NOT an additional IA threshold; it is listed here only so it is not confused with 65.91/65.93.

7. APPLICANT / HOLDER PROCEDURE (how to apply the above)
  Step 1 — Classify the work. Is it a major alteration under 14 CFR 1.1 and Appendix A to Part 43? If no, an IA is not required; a rated mechanic may handle it within 43.3/43.7 privileges.
  Step 2 — Confirm the data. Was the alteration accomplished per technical data approved by the Administrator? If not, the IA may not approve it for return to service under 65.95(a)(1); the data must first be approved through the appropriate FAA process.
  Step 3 — Confirm the aircraft category. If the aircraft is maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, the 65.95(a)(1) privilege is not available; a different authorized approval path applies.
  Step 4 — Inspect for conformity to the approved data and for safe condition, then approve for return to service and sign the record.
  Step 5 — Record the major alteration on FAA Form 337 per Appendix B to Part 43 and ensure the record content of 43.9 is met.
  For eligibility (a new applicant): verify 65.91(c)(1) both ratings current -> (c)(2) 3 years actively engaged -> (c)(3) fixed base -> (c)(4) equipment/facilities/inspection data -> (c)(5) written test passed.
  For renewal: verify 65.92 expiration date (March 31 of odd-numbered years) and the 65.93(b) activity showing (including the 'at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days' standard) plus the continuing mechanic-certificate currency in 65.93(a).

8. CITATION TABLE (verify each at ecfr.gov)
  | Topic | Citation |
  | Definition of major alteration | 14 CFR 1.1 |
  | List of major alterations | 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A |
  | Who may perform alterations | 14 CFR 43.3 |
  | Who may approve for return to service | 14 CFR 43.7 |
  | Maintenance record content | 14 CFR 43.9 |
  | Performance standards | 14 CFR 43.13 |
  | Form 337 recording of major repairs/alterations | 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix B |
  | Mechanic recent experience (separate) | 14 CFR 65.83 |
  | IA eligibility, including major-alteration test element | 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)-(5) |
  | IA duration/expiration | 14 CFR 65.92 |
  | IA renewal / recent major-alteration activity | 14 CFR 65.93 |
  | IA privileges and limitations (major alteration approval) | 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) |

9. GUIDANCE (NON-BINDING — supplements but does not replace the regulation)
  FAA Inspection Authorization Information Guide (faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/ia_info_guide.pdf) — describes the IA's practical role of determining airworthiness by inspecting for conformity to approved data and safe condition.
  AC 43-210A — Standardized Procedures for Obtaining Approval of Data Used in the Performance of Major Repairs and Major Alterations (relevant to the 'approved technical data' condition in 65.95(a)(1)).
  FAA Order 8900.1 (Flight Standards Information Management System) — inspector guidance; internal, not regulatory.
  ACs and orders may be cited to explain practice, but the qualifications and privileges themselves are the CFR sections above.

10. CURRENCY AND VERIFICATION NOTES
  - eCFR is the authoritative current source. Before relying on this in an enforcement, airworthiness, or certification decision, open each cited section at ecfr.gov and confirm (a) the eCFR 'current as of' date and (b) the verbatim paragraph text.
  - Items labeled [paraphrase] above are summarized from the regulation, not quoted; the two quoted passages (65.93(b)(2) and 65.95(a)(1)) were taken from the fetched eCFR page.
  - No dollar values, question counts, or derived multi-year activity totals are asserted here, because none are established by the grounding; the only numeric standards stated are the regulatory ones: 3-year eligibility lookback (65.91(c)(2)), March 31 of odd-numbered years (65.92), and two major repairs or major alterations per 90 days (65.93(b)(2)).

BOTTOM LINE
The qualifications bearing on major alterations are: (1) hold a current A&P mechanic certificate with both ratings; (2) three years actively engaged in maintaining certificated aircraft; (3) a fixed base of operations; (4) available equipment, facilities, and inspection data; (5) pass the written test covering return to service after major repairs and major alterations under Part 43 — 14 CFR 65.91(c)(1)-(5); maintained through the biennial renewal cycle of 65.92/65.93, including the recent major repair/major alteration activity standard. The resulting authority is the 65.95(a)(1) privilege to inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration accomplished per approved technical data, excluding aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
